extracted.intended_audience: citizens, political reformers, and readers concerned with forming constitutions and representative governments (late-18th-century revolutionary/public audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and practical principles for establishing constitutions and representative republican governments: what a republic is, why representation is preferable, how constitutions should be made and revised, and what limits and duties government must observe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic as purpose (res-publica) not a specific form
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called a republic is not any particular form of government. It is wholly characteristical of the purport, matter or object for which government ought to be instituted ... Res-Publica, the public affairs, or the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A republic is defined by government being conducted for the interest of the public (individually and collectively). It is contrasted with monarchy, which makes the ruler himself the object. Anti-pattern: calling a government a 'republic' while it serves private/arbitrary interests (e.g., hereditary aristocracy calling itself a republic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative system as natural protector of the res-publica
rubrics_metrics.description: It most naturally associates with the representative form, as being best calculated to secure the end for which a nation is at the expense of supporting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation is favored because it best secures the public business; examples: America is cited as the only real republic in character and practice. Anti-patterns: simple democracy without representation on large scales; calling aristocratic or hereditary systems 'republics' in name only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use representation to scale democracy to large populations/territories
rubrics_metrics.description: By ingrafting representation upon democracy, we arrive at a system of government capable of embracing and confederating all the various interests and every extent of territory and population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative government remedies the inability of simple democracy to manage large/populous societies. Example: Athens in miniature vs America in magnitude. Monarchy/aristocracy are inadequate substitutes because of ignorance/incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must make the public good its whole object
rubrics_metrics.description: Every government that does not act on the principle of a Republic, or in other words, that does not make the res-publica its whole and sole object, is not a good government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for judging governments: whether they prioritize public affairs and public good rather than private/arbitrary power. Anti-pattern: governments prioritizing ruler's interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegated power is trust; assumed power is usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: All power exercised over a nation, must have some beginning. It must either be delegated or assumed. ... All delegated power is trust, and all assumed power is usurpation. Time does not alter the nature and quality of either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for legitimacy: authority must be delegated by the people; assumed authority is illegitimate even if long-standing. Implication: governments cannot acquire rightful power simply by holding it over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution distinct from government; constitution precedes and controls government
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution is not the act of a government, but of a people constituting a government; and government without a constitution, is power without a right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitution creates and limits government; it is antecedent and superior to the government it establishes. Anti-pattern: treating parliamentary acts or assumed governance as a constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions should never be altered at the discretion of the instituted government
rubrics_metrics.description: No article of this constitution could be altered or infringed at the discretion of the government that was to ensue. It was to that government a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit government from modifying its own constituting instrument. Example: Pennsylvania's constitution provision that only a convention elected by the people may revise the constitution every seven years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution-making process: public drafting, publication, popular conventions and ratification
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention having met and deliberated... they next ordered it to be published, not as a thing established, but for the consideration of the whole people, their approbation or rejection ... the convention then appointed a day for the general election of the representatives ... and having done this they dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete procedural rubric: draft by elected delegates/convention, publish proposed constitution for public consideration, convene popular conventions in the states (or equivalent jurisdictions) for ratification, then proceed to elections under the new constitution. Anti-pattern: secret cabals or governments making constitutions for themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution content elements (minimal checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this constitution were laid down, first, a declaration of rights; then followed the form which the government should have, and the powers it should possess--the authority of the courts of judicature, and of juries--the manner in which elections should be conducted, and the proportion of representatives to the number of electors--the time which each succeeding assembly should continue ... the mode of levying, and of accounting for the expenditure, of public money--of appointing public officers, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should explicitly state: declaration of rights; governmental form; distribution and limits of powers; judicial authority; election rules and representation ratios; term lengths; fiscal rules and accounting; appointment procedures. Use as checklist when drafting or evaluating a constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic revision of constitutions by popular convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution provided that, at the expiration of every seven years, a convention should be elected, for the express purpose of revising the constitution, and making alterations, additions, or abolitions therein, if any such should be found necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow periodic, people-driven revision to incorporate experience and correct errors; avoid permanence that preserves defects. Example: Pennsylvania's seven-year review provision. Anti-pattern: entrenching immutable provisions without means of legitimate amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must not be a party to forming or changing its constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Government has no right to make itself a party in any debate respecting the principles or modes of forming, or of changing, constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent conflict of interest: those exercising governmental power should not control the rules that constrain them. Constituting and amendment power belongs to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: The constituting power is the people; the constitution is property of the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution is the property of a nation, and not of those who exercise the government. All the constitutions of America are declared to be established on the authority of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy derives from popular authority; constitutions should be framed and owned by the populace rather than by governing elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government concentrates necessary practical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It concentrates the knowledge necessary to the interest of the parts, and of the whole. It places government in a state of constant maturity. It is, as has already been observed, never young, never old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation pools local and practical expertise across society, preventing the ignorance of centralized hereditary rulers and the disorder of pure democracy. Use representation to connect diverse interests and practical knowledge to central governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hereditary succession and child/regency rule as contrary to proper government
rubrics_metrics.description: Much less could it [monarchy] when made hereditary. This is the most effectual of all forms to preclude knowledge. ... It is subject neither to nonage, nor dotage. It admits not of a separation between knowledge and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary rule places unfit or immature persons in supreme power, producing ignorance, regencies, intrigue, and instability. Anti-patterns: hereditary monarchies, regencies, and any system that entrusts national governance to accident of birth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should be transparent; republicans reject court secrecy and mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: In the representative system, the reason for everything must publicly appear. Every man is a proprietor in government... There is no place for mystery; nowhere for it to begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is an evaluative criterion: public visibility of reasons and costs prevents imposition and excessive revenues. Secrecy is condemned as enabling court craft and imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government in a free country resides in laws, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of a free country, properly speaking, is not in the persons, but in the laws. The enacting of those requires no great expense; and when they are administered, the whole of civil government is performed--the rest is all court contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether authority is rule-of-law based, with laws publicly known and administered, rather than personalized power or extravagant court structures. Fiscal implication: a law-based government is economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of government expenditure as a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole expense of the federal government of America ... is but six hundred thousand dollars ... To assign a reason for this, appears almost impossible. The generality of people in America, especially the poor, are more able to pay taxes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governments by their cost and tax burden; representative republics should be markedly more economical than monarchic civil lists and court expenditures. Anti-pattern: extravagant civil lists serving a single ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate qualifications for office to ensure maturity and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: In the American Federal Government, more power is delegated to the President of the United States than to any other individual member of Congress. He cannot, therefore, be elected to this office under the age of thirty-five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set age and other qualification thresholds for high office to ensure maturity and knowledge. Contrast with hereditary monarchies that may place adolescents in supreme office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule in representative decision-making with expectation of practical support
rubrics_metrics.description: Such is the nature of representative government, that it quietly decides all matters by majority. ... the objecting members ... said ... they should give it the same practical support as if they had for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative systems resolve disputes by majority vote and demand that minority dissenters accept and support collectively binding decisions to maintain order and functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal powers should be defined and consented to by constituent states
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress first informed the several states, of the powers which it conceived were necessary to be invested in the union, to enable it to perform the duties and services required from it; and the states severally agreed with each other, and concentrated in congress those powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming a federal constitution, enumerate and agree upon the powers to be vested in a central government through the consent of constituent polities (states), rather than allowing a central body to assume power to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political language and labels must match practice (avoid nominal republics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various forms of government have affected to style themselves a republic. Poland calls itself a republic, which is an hereditary aristocracy ... Holland calls itself a republic, which is chiefly aristocratical ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governments by their real character and practice, not by the labels they adopt. A state's name as 'republic' is insufficient; check structural features and who the government actually serves.
